n: Jacob continues with Isaiah 50. The Lord asks Israel: did I divorce you or sell you to pay a debt? No — Israel’s own sins caused the separation. The Book of Mormon adds an opening question, “have I cast thee off forever?”, sharpening the point that God has not abandoned them.

f.g: A legal divorce certificate under the law of Moses.

f.w: for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves

n: When the Lord came, no one answered. Yet His arm is not too short to save. He who can dry up the sea and rivers by His command can certainly redeem Israel. The Book of Mormon makes the first lines statements rather than questions and adds “O house of Israel.”
God can darken the heavens as if dressed in sackcloth, the rough cloth worn in mourning. Some see a foreshadowing of the darkness at Christ’s death.

f.g: Coarse, dark goat-hair cloth worn in grief or repentance.

f.w: I clothe the heavens with blackness

n: Now the Servant speaks. God gave Him a trained tongue to speak the right word to the weary, and wakes Him each morning to listen like a disciple. Christians see Jesus here, whose words strengthened the weary.

f.g: The tongue of one who has been taught — a disciple’s tongue.

n: The Servant listened and did not rebel or turn back — perfect obedience.
The Servant willingly endured beating, having His beard torn, shame, and spitting. This matches Jesus’ sufferings before His crucifixion in striking detail.

f.w: I gave my back to the smiter

f.g: Tore out the beard — a deep insult.

n: Because God helps Him, the Servant will not be put to shame. He sets His face “like a flint” — unshakably determined.

f.w: set my face like a flint

n: The Lord is near and will vindicate Him. Who dares accuse Him? The Book of Mormon adds that He will strike His adversary with the strength of His mouth — His word.
All who condemn the Servant will wear out like an old moth-eaten garment.
Who among you fears the Lord, obeys His servant, yet walks in darkness without light? The Book of Mormon ends the verse here, without the KJV’s added counsel to “trust in the name of the Lord.”
Those who try to light their own way — relying on their own “sparks” rather than God’s light — will lie down in sorrow.

f.w: walk in the light of your fire
